Title: VizLens: A Robust and Interactive Screen Reader for Interfaces in the Real World
Authors: Anhong Guo; Xiang 'Anthony' Chen; Haoran Qi; Samuel White; Suman Ghosh; Chieko Asakawa; Jeffrey P. Bigham
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 29th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '16), pp. 651-664
Research area: CV + crowdsourcing for access to physical appliance interfaces
Problem addressed: Blind people cannot use flat, unlabeled appliance control panels (microwaves, etc.).
Target population: Formative: 1 home observation + 6 blind interviewees (34-73). Evaluation: 10 VI users (21-47), mostly blind/light perception.
Methodology: Blind user photographs panel -> Mechanical Turk workers verify image quality, box and label each control -> reference image; at use time, SURF feature matching + RANSAC homography registers live video, skin-colour fingertip detection, speaks label under finger (feedback mode) or directs finger (guidance mode). Extensions: VizLens::State (multi-screen), ::LCD (OCR).
Technology: Smartphone camera, remote GPU server, crowdsourcing, VoiceOver.
Main findings: Button identification accuracy 96.0%; locating completion 82% (feedback) vs 98% (guidance); crowd labels 99.7% correct, ~8 min, ~US$1.15 per interface; 56.7% of blind users' photos failed quality check; ~8 fps, ~200 ms latency.
Limitations: Fails on interfaces with few visual features; hand occlusion; skin-coloured buttons; camera aiming hard for blind users; needs network/remote GPU at every use; deliberately does NOT modify the physical interface (no tactile output).
Research gaps: Requires the phone and connectivity at every interaction; no permanent physical/tactile mapping; not evaluated on wall switches.
Relevance to SPARSH: Closest CV precedent. SPARSH differs: sighted caregiver (not blind user) captures photo; on-device/one-time CV with human confirmation instead of crowd; output is a permanent physical tactile layer used offline daily.
Design implications: Expect poor photos -> add capture guidance and quality check; human labelling of controls is accurate (crowd 99.7%) so a caregiver-confirm step is well-founded; one-time setup avoids VizLens' per-use latency.

Title: ApplianceReader: A Wearable, Crowdsourced, Vision-based System to Make Appliances Accessible
Authors: Anhong Guo; Xiang 'Anthony' Chen; Jeffrey P. Bigham
Journal/conference: CHI '15 Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 2043-2048
Research area: Wearable CV for appliance access (precursor to VizLens)
Problem addressed: Flat appliance control panels make blind users dependent on others.
Target population: Home observation/interview with a VI person (formative).
Methodology: Work-in-progress: Google Glass camera; crowd outlines and labels controls once; CV matches live view and announces button under fingertip via TTS.
Main findings: Prototype ran at ~2 fps (640x360) on a laptop; identified photo-quality and lighting challenges; proposed falling back to live crowd help when recognition confidence is low; suggested shared libraries of labelled appliances.
Relevance to SPARSH: Early statement of 'label once, reuse' and of confidence-based fallback to humans - both core SPARSH ideas.
Design implications: Use confidence thresholds to route uncertain detections to the caregiver; consider a shared library of common Indian switch-plate layouts.

Title: StateLens: A Reverse Engineering Solution for Making Existing Dynamic Touchscreens Accessible
Authors: Anhong Guo; Junhan Kong; Michael Rivera; Frank F. Xu; Jeffrey P. Bigham
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 32nd Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '19), pp. 371-385
Problem addressed: Dynamic, multi-screen touchscreens (kiosks, coffee machines) are inaccessible to blind people.
Target population: Blind users in a system study (count not verified).
Methodology: Hybrid crowd + CV reconstruction of interface state diagrams from point-of-view videos; conversational agent guidance in iOS app; 3D-printed accessories to explore touchscreens without accidental touches.
Main findings: Accurately reconstructed interfaces from stationary, hand-held and web videos; user study indicated blind users could access previously inaccessible interfaces (quantitative values not verified).
Limitations: Target is touchscreens, not mechanical switches.
Relevance to SPARSH: Shows the research line combining CV with 3D-printed physical aids; SPARSH targets static mechanical switchboards, which are simpler and suit one-time mapping.
Design implications: Static switchboards allow a one-time map; no need for state tracking.

Title: Evaluating Author and User Experience for an Audio-Haptic System for Annotation of Physical Models
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 19th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '17), pp. 369-370
Research area: Sighted-authored audio annotations on physical objects (CamIO)
Problem addressed: Making physical models/objects self-describing for blind users.
Target population: 3 blind volunteers; focus group of 5 blind adults; 1 sighted annotator.
Methodology: Formative studies of CamIO: sighted assistant clicks hotspots on two images and types labels (Creator); blind user's fingertip tracked by webcam and labels spoken (Explorer).
Technology: Laptop webcam, fiducial board, fingertip marker, TTS.
Main findings: Blind participants read hotspots independently; focus group named appliance access as a use case and valued annotation that separates accessibility from the object's original design; sighted annotator needed ~5-10 min per object.
Limitations: Very small samples; no accuracy data; marker visibility problems.
Relevance to SPARSH: Close analogue of SPARSH's 'sighted person authors once, blind person uses' division of labour.
Design implications: Budget ~5-10 min caregiver authoring time as a usability target.

Title: You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection
Authors: Joseph Redmon; Santosh Divvala; Ross Girshick; Ali Farhadi
Journal/conference: 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 779-788
Methodology: Single-network detector (details per original paper; not re-verified here).
Main findings: Foundational single-stage real-time detector family that later YOLO versions build on.
Relevance to SPARSH: Candidate detector family for switch detection; needs labelled switchboard images.
Design implications: If using YOLO, fine-tune from pretrained weights on a small, team-collected Indian switchboard dataset; report precision/recall per class.

Title: Deep Learning vs. Traditional Computer Vision
Authors: Niall O'Mahony; Sean Campbell; Anderson Carvalho; Suman Harapanahalli; Gustavo Velasco Hernandez; Lenka Krpalkova; Daniel Riordan; Joseph Walsh
Journal/conference: Advances in Computer Vision (CVC 2019), Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing, pp. 128-144 (online 2019)
Main findings: Argues classical CV remains relevant and hybrid methods can outperform or handle problems DL does not suit well.
Limitations: Abstract does not state small-data criteria explicitly (not verified).
Relevance to SPARSH: Supports SPARSH considering a classical (edge/contour/template) or hybrid baseline for highly regular switchboards with little training data.
Design implications: Report a classical baseline (e.g., contour detection of rectangular rocker switches) alongside any learned detector.

Title: VizWiz: Nearly Real-time Answers to Visual Questions
Authors: Jeffrey P. Bigham; Chandrika Jayant; Hanjie Ji; Greg Little; Andrew Miller; Robert C. Miller; Robin Miller; Aubrey Tatarowicz; Brandyn White; Samual White; Tom Yeh
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 23rd Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '10), pp. 333-342
Research area: Crowd-powered visual assistance for blind people
Problem addressed: Blind people need answers about visual content in near real-time.
Relevance to SPARSH: Origin of the photo-then-human-answers paradigm underlying VizLens/Facade.

Title: VizWiz Grand Challenge: Answering Visual Questions from Blind People
Authors: Danna Gurari; Qing Li; Abigale J. Stangl; Anhong Guo; Chi Lin; Kristen Grauman; Jiebo Luo; Jeffrey P. Bigham
Journal/conference: 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 3608-3617
Problem addressed: CV models are trained on well-composed photos unlike those taken by blind people.
Target population: Blind smartphone users who submitted photos/questions.
Methodology: Dataset of >31,000 visual questions with 10 crowd answers each.
Main findings: Photos by blind photographers are often poor quality and questions often unanswerable.
Relevance to SPARSH: Supports SPARSH's choice that a sighted caregiver, not the blind user, takes the setup photo.
Design implications: Still add capture guidance (framing, glare check) for caregivers; detection must tolerate oblique angles and reflections on glossy plates.
